staged_description.title: Family Separation Return - 'Zero Tolerance' Policy Reinstatement
staged_description.description_short: Family Separation Return - 'Zero Tolerance' Policy Reinstatement
staged_description.description_medium: Donald Trump refused to rule out reinstating his family separation policy during the 2024 campaign and moved to revive elements of the practice after returning to office, despite the 'national uproar' it had created when thousands of children were separated from their parents at the southern border during his first presidency.
staged_description.description_long: Donald Trump refused to rule out reinstating his family separation policy during the 2024 campaign and moved to revive elements of the practice after returning to office, despite the 'national uproar' it had created when thousands of children were separated from their parents at the southern border during his first presidency. Trump defended family separations as effective deterrents, claiming in November 2023 that 'when you hear you're going to be separated from your family, you don't come' and that 'it stopped people from coming by the hundreds of thousands.' His administration began terminating the Flores Settlement Agreement in May 2025, which had provided protections for migrant children in detention, while moving toward policies that would allow prolonged family detention and separation. Despite legal settlements requiring family reunification from his first term, indications emerged that family separation could return as Trump prioritized what he called deterrence over keeping families together. The administration's motion to terminate Flores claimed the agreement 'removes the disincentives enacted by Congress' and argued against protections that prevented long-term detention of children. While some former Trump officials expressed wariness about full reinstatement due to the previous 'national uproar,' Trump's continued defense of the policy and systematic dismantling of child protection agreements suggested family separations remained part of his immigration strategy.

Separately, a Higher Education Policy Institute account said the administration sent warning letters to 60 universities.

The systematic university control represented unprecedented federal interference in higher education autonomy, transforming institutions from centers of learning and inquiry into vehicles for advancing conservative ideology while eliminating programs that had expanded educational access and opportunity for historically marginalized communities.

staged_description.description_long: Maryland and Prince George’s County sued the Trump administration on November 6, 2025, over its decision to keep the FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C., rather than move it to Greenbelt. The General Services Administration had selected Greenbelt in 2023 after years of study and competition among Maryland and Virginia sites, and local officials said the state and county had made extensive preparations. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Maryland, asks the court to stop the selection of the Reagan Building and prevent the transfer of the designated funds. A Senate committee had recently advanced a plan to keep the FBI in Washington, estimating nearly $1.4 billion for the Reagan Building project. Brown described the administration’s reversal as unlawful; at the time of the announcement, the claims were allegations in a newly filed case, not a court ruling.

staged_description.description_short: Trump orders drone strike that kills Iranian General Qasem Soleimani
staged_description.description_medium: On January 3, 2020, the United States killed Iranian General Qasem Soleimani in a drone strike near Baghdad airport on orders from President Trump. The strike escalated tensions with Iran, sparked fears of wider conflict, and raised questions about legal authority and congressional oversight. The killing was widely described as a major escalation in U.S.–Iran confrontation.
staged_description.description_long: A U.S. drone strike near Baghdad International Airport killed Iranian Major General Qasem Soleimani on January 3, 2020. Soleimani commanded the Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which conducts the group’s operations abroad. President Trump ordered the strike. The administration said it was intended to deter future attacks, while critics questioned the evidence for an imminent threat, the legal basis for using force, and whether Congress should have authorized the operation. Because the strike took place on Iraqi territory, it also raised questions about Iraq’s sovereignty and the risks to U.S. forces and partners in the region. Soleimani’s death sharply escalated the confrontation between Washington and Tehran and prompted fears of retaliation and wider conflict. The operation became one of the most consequential uses of U.S. force during Trump’s first term, bringing presidential war powers and congressional oversight into renewed focus. The competing arguments over the strike’s justification remained central to the political debate that followed.

staged_description.title: Ends DACA Program for Dreamers
staged_description.description_short: The administration announced it would end DACA, the program protecting undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children, jeopardizing hundreds of thousands of Dreamers.
staged_description.description_medium: On September 5, 2017, the Trump administration announced the rescission of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), the policy that had provided renewable deferred action and work authorization to certain people brought to the United States as children. The memorandum set a wind-down rather than immediately canceling every existing grant: most current protections remained through their expiration dates, and a limited window was allowed for certain renewal applications. It stopped accepting new initial requests after the announcement.
staged_description.description_long: On September 5, 2017, the Department of Homeland Security announced that it would rescind Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA. Established in 2012, the policy had allowed eligible people brought to the United States as children to request renewable periods of deferred action and employment authorization. The administration said it was ending the policy after a legal assessment by the attorney general. The rescission memorandum did not cancel every existing grant on announcement day. DHS said it would generally leave current grants in place until their expiration and created a limited renewal window for certain beneficiaries whose protections were due to expire between September 5, 2017, and March 5, 2018. Renewal requests in that group had to be accepted by October 5, 2017. DHS stopped accepting new initial applications after September 5, while applications already accepted by that date could still be considered case by case. The announcement placed hundreds of thousands of DACA recipients' future status in doubt, but the policy's effects were not immediate or uniform: existing grants continued temporarily, and the memorandum's timetable was subsequently affected by litigation. The linked DHS memorandum was inaccessible during this pass; this description follows the dated rescission memorandum as summarized in the official court record and distinguishes the announced wind-down from an immediate termination of all protections.

staged_description.description_short: Trump signed legislation to nullify the Stream Protection Rule, rolling back Obama-era protections for streams near coal mining operations.
staged_description.description_medium: On February 16, 2017, President Donald Trump signed H.J. Res. 38, a Congressional Review Act resolution that nullified the Interior Department’s Stream Protection Rule. The 2016 rule set requirements for protecting streams and groundwater from impacts associated with surface coal mining. With the resolution enacted, the rule had no force or effect, and the agency could not issue a substantially similar rule without further congressional authorization under the act.

The U.S. Supreme Court later reversed the result in Trump v. The case became a national test of how the post-Civil War amendment could apply to presidential candidates and who had authority to enforce it. The Supreme Court’s decision resolved the ballot question but did not endorse the events of January 6 or decide every constitutional question surrounding Section 3. This context distinguishes the Colorado court’s disqualification ruling from the later federal decision that removed its practical effect.
